text:
Ah, the candle. That humble cylinder of solidified animal fat or petroleum byproduct, wrapped in a twisted cotton wick, standing as the ultimate symbol of modern sophistication. It is not merely a source of light; it is a beacon of "ambiance," a fragile testament to our collective inability to afford electricity or basic interior design.

The primary material? Wax. Specifically, the kind that melts into a puddle of regret if you look at it wrong, or worse, if you leave it unattended for more than three seconds. It is a substance designed to slowly consume itself in a dramatic display of thermal decay, all while emitting a scent of "vanilla bean" that smells suspiciously like a chemical factory had a romantic encounter with a bakery. We pay a premium for this slow-burning disaster, calling it "self-care," when in reality, it is just a controlled fire hazard that makes your apartment smell like a department store’s clearance section. Truly, the pinnacle of adulting: lighting a stick of melted plastic to pretend you have your life together while you stare blankly at a wall, wondering if you remembered to pay the electric bill.
